Cybertruck Could Get Trick Suspension-Based Loading Ramp

MR
By Marco Rossi Senior Supercar & Aerodynamics Editor • via Carscoops Wire
⚡ Visual Story
Source & Photography: Carscoops Wire Dispatch Verified Editorial Asset
⚡ Executive Takeaways & Key Highlights
  • Loading a truck can be tricky if the cargo is heavy or awkward, like with a motorcycle.
  • Tesla might have a novel solution, based on a patent application published a week ago that puts the trick suspension system in the Cybertruck — including the new low-cost model — to work.
  • Official reporting verified via Carscoops news desk.
⚡ EDITORIAL TAKE • MARCO ROSSI Senior Supercar & Aerodynamics Editor

The Benchmark for Track-Tolerant Engineering

In the high-stakes supercar arena, pure horsepower is no longer enough to claim supremacy. This dispatch from Carscoops emphasizes how cutting-edge downforce balance, electronic limited-slip differentials, and hybrid torque-vectoring are reshaping driver engagement. Exotic marques must prove that extreme performance can harmonize with reliability, thermal endurance, and road compliance.

Big Picture: Lap times at benchmark proving grounds and early client allocations will reveal whether this performance envelope disrupts the existing supercar hierarchy.

Loading a truck can be tricky if the cargo is heavy or awkward, like with a motorcycle. Tesla might have a novel solution, based on a patent application published a week ago that puts the trick suspension system in the Cybertruck — including the new low-cost model — to work. At the owner's command, it would raise the front of the truck, lower the rear, and make access to the bed that much easier. Patent application number US 2026/0326744 A1, titled 'Adjustable Suspension For A Vehicle', details a 'ramp mode' that independently adjusts the suspension at each wheel.

📌 The Core Development

The drawings use the familiar wedge-shaped pickup, but it's worth noting that Tesla describes the technology broadly rather than exclusively for the Cybertruck. Tilting the truck changes the angle where a ramp would meet the bed, which could make loading an ATV or motorcycle easier. Tesla also says lowering the rear would allow owners to use a shorter ramp. In one example, the automaker proposes raising the front of the truck by 80 mm (3.1 inches) while lowering the rear by 70 mm (2.8 inches) to reduce the ramp-to-bed breakover angle.

🔍 Background & Sector Context

Tilting the bed sounds reasonable, but the payoff is in how much it changes the loading equation. According to Tesla, the angle where the ramp meets the bed could drop from 45–55 degrees to 20–30 degrees. Tesla says owners would be able to adjust individual corners of the suspension on uneven ground and control everything from an onboard interface or smartphone. Included safeguards would keep the vehicle in Park, automatically apply the parking brake, and prevent shifts into Drive, Reverse, or Neutral while 'ramp mode' is active.

📊 Industry & Real-World Impact

Sensor inputs could block or delay a suspension adjustment if conditions make it unsuitable. Other proposed settings include a 'dump mode', which lowers all four corners to bring the truck bed within easier reach, and a leveling mode intended for activities such as camping or tailgating on uneven ground. Interestingly, in November 2019, Tesla filed a patent application for an adjustable vehicle suspension. It featured similar ideas, so in a way, this is the company simply continuing the slow march toward patent acquisition and potentially production.

🔮 Strategic Outlook & What Lies Ahead

Of course, a key point here is that this is just a patent application. Like plenty of other patent applications, there's no telling if this ever makes it into production. That said, when we uncovered patents for Tesla's fan-assisted suction system and adjustable rear spoiler for the Roadster around a month ago, the company confirmed both were slated for production during the wild Roadster demo in mid-October. Those were practical engineering exercises and this new way of loading a bed seems to follow in line.
